overview:
Lebanon is a small country on the eastern shore of the Mediterranean Sea, smaller than Connecticut, wedged between Syria and Israel. Two mountain ranges run its whole length parallel to the coast, with the fertile Bekaa Valley between them; from the higher slopes it is possible to ski in the morning and swim in the sea the same afternoon. Beirut, the capital, is a port city that has been destroyed and rebuilt many times over its long history.

About 5.5 million people live in Lebanon, along with many refugees from Syria and Palestinians whose families arrived decades ago. Arabic is the official language, French and English are widely spoken, and many Lebanese slide between all three in a single sentence. Lebanon is a republic whose top offices are shared among religious communities: the president is a Maronite Christian, the prime minister a Sunni Muslim, and the speaker of parliament a Shia Muslim. Banking, farming and Lebanese families abroad shape the economy.
landAndNature: The Mount Lebanon range rises steeply from the coast to Qurnat as Sawda at about 3,088 meters and keeps its snow into spring, while the Anti-Lebanon range marks the Syrian border. Between them lies the Bekaa Valley, a fertile trough of vineyards, wheat and orchards. The cedar of Lebanon, a broad, flat-topped tree that can live more than a thousand years, appears on the national flag; ancient groves such as the Cedars of God survive in mountain pockets after centuries of logging. Jeita Grotto is a vast limestone cave with an underground river that visitors travel by boat. Wild boar, hyenas and migrating birds cross the highlands.
peopleAndCulture: Lebanese food travels the world: hummus, tabbouleh, kibbeh and grilled meats arrive as mezze, dozens of small dishes shared slowly around a table. Meals can stretch for hours, and hospitality is close to obligatory. Christians and Muslims of many denominations live side by side, so the calendar carries both Christmas and Ramadan. Fairuz, a singer beloved across the Arab world, plays in Beirut cafes most mornings. Poetry, publishing and journalism have long been Lebanese strengths, and the country has one of the highest literacy rates in the region. Basketball is enormously popular, alongside soccer and winter skiing.
history: The Phoenicians built Lebanon's coastal cities, including Byblos, Tyre and Sidon, more than 3,000 years ago, traded across the Mediterranean and spread an alphabet that became the ancestor of many written scripts used today. Romans raised the enormous temples at Baalbek. Later came Arab rule, crusader castles, and four centuries within the Ottoman Empire. France governed Lebanon after World War I, and independence came in 1943. A civil war among the country's communities, drawing in outside powers, lasted from 1975 to 1990 and left Beirut divided and scarred. In August 2020 a huge explosion of chemicals stored at Beirut's port killed more than 200 people and damaged much of the city.
funFacts: The Phoenician alphabet, developed in Lebanon's coastal cities, is an ancestor of the Greek, Latin and many other alphabets.
Byblos has been lived in for roughly 7,000 years and is among the oldest continuously inhabited cities on Earth.
The cedar of Lebanon on the national flag can live over a thousand years and spreads wide, flat branches.
On some spring days Lebanese people ski in the mountains in the morning and swim in the Mediterranean that afternoon.
Baalbek's Roman temple platform contains some of the largest cut stone blocks ever moved, each weighing hundreds of tons.
